extracted.intended_audience: creative writers, literary critics, and general readers interested in style, moral imagination, and cultural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting imaginative, moral, and stylistically clear prose that balances reverence and irreverence, designs fixed artistic proportions, sustains real stakes, and preserves wonder. Emphasises plain language, levity, and vigilance against complacent novelty or facile sentimentalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composite balance of reverence and disdain
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal attitude must combine 'a certain amount of restraint and respect, a certain amount of energy and mastery' and 'must have in us enough reverence for all things outside us... [and] enough disdain for all things outside us'—a precise proportion of humility and audacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for a single, particular proportion of wonder and defiance in tone and characterization: characters should be humble enough to marvel yet proud enough to act. Chesterton illustrates this with the fairy-tale idea that the prince must be 'at once humble enough to wonder, and haughty enough to defy.' Avoid one-sided sentimental tenderness or pure contempt; the best fiction holds both in a specific balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fix the ideal (avoid drift)
rubrics_metrics.description: First requirement: 'it must be fixed' — an ideal or artistic goal should be determinate rather than a mere impersonal trend or drift.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When shaping a work, define a stable, articulate conception of its moral or aesthetic aim (a 'fixed' ideal) rather than relying on vague evolutionary/trend-like progress. Chesterton contrasts a fixed, designed happiness with a simple biological drift that cannot account for proportion or purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design proportions deliberately (only a mind can place them)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proportion 'cannot be a drift: it is either an accident or a design... if this composite happiness is fixed for us it must be fixed by some mind; for only a mind can place the exact proportions of a composite happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose your work with deliberate attention to the relative weight of its elements (humour, seriousness, adventure, tenderness). Treat balance as an act of design: arrange scenes, motifs, and character traits intentionally rather than allowing them to 'evolve' accidentally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain vigilance; preserve institutions and stakes
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave things alone and they change; 'if you leave a thing alone you leave it to a torrent of change... If you particularly want it to be white you must be always painting it again; that is, you must be always having a revolution.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In worldbuilding and plot, recognise the need for active maintenance—institutions, rules, and moral constraints must be tended. Avoid utopias in which ties, obligations, or consequences dissolve; instead dramatise the work required to keep values alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism of novelty-as-improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'We have not any need to rebel against antiquity; we have to rebel against novelty.' Novelty or 'the new' does not automatically equal progress or moral improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not valorise change for its own sake in theme or plot. Question whether innovations in society or character actually serve moral ends; show how new systems can become oppressive as readily as old ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short/plain words to force thought
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton recommends expressing opinions 'in words of one syllable' as an exercise: 'The long words are not the hard words, it is the short words that are hard.' Short, concrete words force the writer and reader to think more clearly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer plain, monosyllabic diction where clarity and force are required; avoid jargon and long, abstract phrases that become 'labour-saving' mental shortcuts. Short words can carry metaphysical subtlety and provoke thought more effectively than pompous long phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid equivocal use of key terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware when the same long word is used to mean different things (e.g., 'idealist' as philosophy vs. moral rhetoric; 'liberal' in theology vs. politics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define or disambiguate important terms in your writing. Do not rely on fashionable words whose meaning shifts by context; clarify which sense you mean to use to avoid misleading or lazy argumentation in fiction or essays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value levity and lightness over mere seriousness
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Seriousness is not a virtue... It is much easier to write a good TIMES leading article than a good joke in PUNCH... In perfect force there is a kind of frivolity... Angels can fly because they can take themselves lightly.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate lightness, humour, and self-forgetfulness in tone and characterisation. Levity is difficult and valuable; don't mistake solemnity for moral depth. Use playful imagery and an airy touch where appropriate to achieve spiritual or aesthetic elevation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make stakes real and irrevocable
rubrics_metrics.description: 'For the purpose even of the wildest romance results must be real; results must be irrevocable.' The romantic or adventurous effect depends on consequences that truly bind and matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that promises, wagers, vows, challenges, and punishments in fiction have meaningful, often irreversible consequences. Avoid depowering plot stakes with easy reversals or conveniences; the poetic power of romance comes from risk and irrevocability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use commitments and vows to generate drama
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I should ask to be kept to my bargain, to have my oaths and engagements taken seriously... Christian marriage is the great example of a real and irrevocable result; and that is why it is the chief subject and centre of all our romantic writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ binding commitments (marriage, oaths, contracts) as structural devices to create moral tension and narrative consequence. Let characters be constrained by the obligations they accept, which in turn drives plot and tragedy/comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embrace wonder and the miraculous as imaginative liberty
rubrics_metrics.description: 'A miracle simply means the swift control of matter by mind... A miracle only means the liberty of God.' Chesterton argues that belief in miracles aligns with a liberal idea of freedom (liberty of the supernatural), not with dogmatic suppression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't dismiss supernatural or improbable elements out of hand; employ wonder or miraculous occurrences to dramatise freedom, agency, and the mind's control over matter. Miracles can function as legitimate imaginative tools, not mere relics of superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray power and wealth skeptically (moral fallibility of rank)
rubrics_metrics.description: Christian dogma 'that any man in any rank may take bribes' and 'to be rich is to be in peculiar danger of moral wreck.' One should not assume that social rank equates to moral trustworthiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depict rulers and the wealthy with moral complexity and susceptibility to corruption; avoid idealising authority. Use character and plot to challenge assumptions that privilege implies virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer leaders who are modest or reluctant
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The man should rule who does NOT think that he can rule... we must crown the much more exceptional man who knows he can't.' Leadership in a moral democracy is better embodied by the modest and unwilling than by the ambitious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing protagonists or moral exemplars, consider reluctant leaders or humble figures as more psychologically and morally credible. Such characters embody a paradoxical strength and fit themes of humility and service.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reframe common metaphors to produce fresh tone (e.g., Nature as sister)
rubrics_metrics.description: Chesterton reframes Nature: 'Nature is not our mother: Nature is our sister... To St. Francis, Nature is a sister, and even a younger sister: a little, dancing sister, to be laughed at as well as loved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use unexpected figurative shifts to change readers' emotional response—recasting the familiar in a new familial relation (mother→sister) alters moral and tonal implications, permitting laughter as well as love. Try small metaphorical reframings to unlock new modes of feeling.
